idiom_name: two classes with mutual references, wired by a static factory (classic Twin)
implementation_notes: C# classes have exactly one base class and interfaces cannot carry instance state, so combining a base class that owns state and behaviour (Thread, a framework view, a lifecycle base) with a second class's code still needs two objects: one class per parent, each holding a reference to its twin, created and linked in a static factory so no half-linked pair escapes. What replaces the classic structure in many cases: C# 8 default interface members let an interface carry behaviour (still no instance state), so a second parent that contributes behaviour only collapses into one class implementing interfaces - and framework parenting that used to be Thread-based is normally Task-based today. Keep the twin when both parents are classes with state you cannot refactor.
pitfalls: internal (assembly) is the narrowest access C# offers across two classes; private cannot be seen by the partner, so the link is either internal or a property that leaks the partner to the whole assembly.
Both ends are reference types: if a framework collection (thread pool, event list, registry) keeps the platform end referenced, the abstraction end stays alive too - clear the link on teardown.
State inherited from a shared base exists twice, once per end: a lock or an identifier 'in the parent' is not shared across the pair, so shared state must be modelled explicitly in one end.

default interface members are callable only through the interface type and must be overridden with explicit interface implementation, so the twin end's implicit implementation of the class-facing member does not satisfy the interface contract.

variants.name: Second capability as an interface with default implementations (C# 8)
variants.idiom_name: one class, second capability modelled as an interface with default implementations
variants.implementation_notes: C# 8 lets an interface carry method bodies with an explicit access modifier, so when the second hierarchy contributes behaviour only, one class can implement the interface and the crossing calls become default members; the interface cannot declare instance fields or auto-properties, so any state requirement forces the classic pair. Use this variant where the second hierarchy is a set of capabilities rather than a stateful class (the ILight/ITimerLight/IBlinkingLight style composition the language docs use for mixins), and remember that default members are reached through the interface reference, not through the class.
pitfalls: Default members are accessible only through the interface type: ball.Toggle() does not compile when ball is typed as the class.
Two derived interfaces providing the same member create an ambiguity the compiler refuses to resolve; keep capability interfaces small and disjoint (the language docs make the same recommendation).
Interfaces cannot hold instance state, and ref struct implementers must declare default members explicitly; do not fake state with static fields when a second stateful parent is needed.
